newsitem.title: USA: Retail sales, not jobs, tops on U.S. bond mkt list.
newsitem.headline: Retail sales, not jobs, tops on U.S. bond mkt list.

text.p: For years, the monthly employment report was treated with so much reverence, the U.S. bond market barely budged in the days prior to its release.
But now, the report has taken a back seat to the monthly retail sales figures. Market participants believe retail sales data, not payrolls, hold the key to future monetary policy.

"Right now, spending is more important," said Cary Leahey, chief U.S. economist at High Frequency Economics. "If it starts turning around (from its recent weak spell), the market will get very nervous."

Players noted that spending data has heavily influenced the Treasury market the past few months. In mid-March, a strong February retail sales report triggered a sell-off, which lasted until a weak March sales report a month later.
With retail sales down in March, April and May, the market has rallied on the view the Federal Reserve is reluctant to tighten further when consumers are not spending.

"From the moment the Fed tightened (in March) for 'persisting strength in demand,' the demand side variables rose over supply side variables," said Paul McCulley, chief economist at UBS Securities LLC.
"Employment is supply side and ... doesn't tell us the outlook for monetary policy," McCulley said.

Clearly, the market agrees. According to GovPX, trading volume in the hour after the monthly employment release has averaged $17.7 billion the past three months. In contrast, volume after retail sales averaged $19.9 billion.
"Employment has been a lousy indicator of inflation as measured by the CPI," said William Lloyd, head of market strategy and credit market research at BZW Securities Inc.
That's not to say the market is shunning employment.
"It is still important; it sets the tone for the month," Leahey said. "But (Fed chairman Alan) Greenspan, in his tightening communique (on March 25), noted demand growth."
As such, the market will probably look past Thursday's release of the June employment report and wait until the June retail sales report will be released on July 15.
Should consumer spending rebound in June and again in July, analysts said the market will start to price in a Fed rate hike once again at the August Fed meeting.

Forecasts said June spending figures should show signs of a rebound. Strong income and job growth, widely available credit and the highest level of consumer confidence in nearly three decades were expected to lead the resurgence.
Some said that while retail sales figures have risen in significance, employment remains the top economic release.
"It is a big mistake to to say retail sales have taken the place as the most important (report)," said Rich Bodkin, head of the government bond desk at First Chicago Capital Markets Inc.
Bodkin resasoned that the market's limited reaction to employment data in recent months was mainly due to jobs reports that were fairly close to consensus and had already been priced in.
As for Thursday's jobs data, traders don't expect a big reaction, since it comes a day after the Fed's meeting and trading desks will be thin ahead of the long holiday weekend.
